Hanging Valleys

The road to Yosemite started under a nearly full moon. Night one was a gravel campsite below a wall of fluted desert cliffs, with the new Jeep parked in the dust. The moon photobombed several of my night shots, but the stars still came through in the ones where it behaved. Then came the valley. At Tunnel View, El Capitan rises on the left and Bridalveil Fall slips down the wall on the right, with Half Dome far back in the haze between them.

Down in the valley, the scale gets ridiculous. Half Dome stood crisp against the blue, almost a mile above the valley floor. The Merced raced clear and fast over its boulders, with the top of El Capitan peeking out above the trees. Yosemite Falls was still thundering in mid-July, high above golden meadows and yellow wildflowers! The waterfalls here leap straight off the cliffs because glaciers carved the main valley so deep that the side creeks were left hanging high on the walls. Geologists call them hanging valleys. For the falls at full strength, go in spring or early summer; by late summer they can shrink to a trickle.

I ended up at the foot of El Capitan, in a boulder field dotted with dead trees, staring up at about 3,000 feet of granite striped with long dark streaks. A contrail slanted toward the rim, as if the plane had a very tall wall to clear. Too many of my pictures from the valley point straight up, because that is where everything is. A contrail lasts a few minutes. A waterfall lasts a season. El Capitan has stood here for millions of years.
